doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Religion, church music and black history
summary: His mother played organ, taught him spirituals and black history, and he stopped attending church once he left.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Was she a very religious woman?
Of course. Religious. Very religious. She went to church four times every Sunday.
Did you have to go to church?
Yeah, I had to go to church. And once I got away from there, I haven’t been to another one.
That’s right. I told my father, once I get away from here, that’s it.
How much music was there in the church apart from your father’s playing organ?
All kind of music. My mother knew more music than anybody I ever met in my life. When I was a little kid, I was singing a lot of stuff that people started singing later on.
We were talking about church. Let’s start from the top. She was an organist, you went to church with her, and she knew all kinds of music.

Yes. All kinds of music. When I was a little kid, I was singing songs like “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” and I knew James Weldon Johnson—I knew about him. FMI(?—13:37), and all that stuff. “Precious Lord” and all those songs that the black composers wrote. I knew all about it. I knew all about Sojourner Truth and Highland Rebels, and all of them...black people after reconstruction. She taught us all of that.
So you learned about black history.
She told us all about black history before I was 5 or 6 years old. We knew all about it.
So her attitude about what you could talk about and couldn’t talk about at the table didn’t correspond to not giving you information about heritage.
Oh, no. I got the information. She gave me information about everything.
